The core insight is that reward timing modulates cognitive demand and behavioral learning efficiency. Immediate reward induces a stronger demand state, leading to faster learning. This can be formalized as a stochastic process where reward delay τ acts as a control parameter. The demand intensity D(τ) decreases exponentially with τ, implying that D(0) > D(τ) for τ > 0. The performance metric P(τ) is inversely related to D(τ), forming a dual relationship. In GSI, this translates into Bayesian updating of belief states over time, where the likelihood function encodes the temporal structure of reward delivery. In GSE, the system evolves through state transitions governed by a Markov kernel that incorporates delay-dependent reward probabilities. The failure mode occurs when delay exceeds a critical threshold, causing convergence to suboptimal policies. Dualities emerge in the form of information-theoretic entropy and reward-based utility functions, both of which exhibit monotonic behavior with respect to τ.
